item.title: Our Interview With María Corina Machado
item.description:
María Corina Machado is Venezuela’s most popular opposition leader. But she has not been able to return to her country since last year, when she left to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Since then, the Trump administration captured Venezuela’s autocratic leader, Nicolás Maduro, on Jan. 3, 2026, and installed his vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, passing over Ms. Machado for the leadership spot.

Ms. Machado’s political movement won Venezuela’s 2024 presidential vote, even as the state arrested, beat and imprisoned her supporters. But the ruling party refused to give up power, and it continues to govern under President Trump.

Ms. Machado wants to return to Venezuela and run for president in another election. She spoke this week with Julie Turkewitz, the Andes bureau chief for The New York Times. They met in Panama, where Ms. Machado is staying.

Here are excerpts from the wide-ranging interview, in which Ms. Machado criticized the Trump administration’s handpicked partner in Venezuela and spoke about her country’s future.

I want to start by talking about where we are now. Have you been sidelined politically by the United States?

This is a really transformational moment. I believe that Venezuela has had a cultural change for the good, even though it went through this ordeal of 27 years, and so much devastation.

What we have done in these last years is something that is unstoppable and irreversible.

So probably we have different time frames with the United States government, but I have no doubt that we have the same vision in terms of a democratic transition. And in that sense, you cannot sideline the will of a people that have decided to be free and that have organized themselves to achieve it.

Do you agree with the decision by the U.S. to keep Delcy Rodríguez in power?

That was a possibility. She’s certainly doing whatever she’s been told. And that can be comfortable for certain interests in terms of moving smoothly.

I believe it could have been done, certainly, without her because she’s part of the criminal system. But it is what it is, and here’s where we are, and as I said before, it’s in the interest of the Venezuelan people that this works.

If you become the next leader of the country, what is your specific plan for what happens to the high-level leaders of the current government? You have talked about the idea of justice. Specifically what does that process look like?

We want Venezuela to change, so something that we certainly will not do is act as the regime has done, violating human rights and violating the Constitution. So certainly, we’re determined to offer justice and respect for the rights of even those people that violated our own rights.

Because this has to be the foundation of an institutional framework that will last for generations to come. So we’re not moved by revenge or hate.

We are moved by the truth and the fact that we have to assure that those crimes will never be repeated in Venezuela.

Our proposal is to create a truth commission that’s integrated by individuals that have respect and credibility in all of Venezuelan society and can address, case by case, how to move forward, taking into account not only the severity, the seriousness of the crimes committed, but also the disposition of every individual to ask for forgiveness, to facilitate the process, to facilitate justice.

Would some of the highest figures — for example Delcy Rodriguez, Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello — face possible prison charges in a new government?

[As vice president under Mr. Maduro, Ms. Rodríguez helped lead a government in which human rights abuses were common. The Trump administration imposed sanctions on her in 2018, calling her a key figure in solidifying Mr. Maduro’s authoritarian rule; it lifted the sanctions this year after choosing her as Venezuela’s leader.

As interior minister in charge of the police and prisons, Mr. Cabello has overseen widespread repression in Venezuela, the U.N. says. The Trump administration imposed sanctions on him as well, and named him as a defendant in a Jan. 3 drug trafficking indictment against Maduro, but he remains in Ms. Rodríguez’s government.]

In our Constitution and international treaties, there are crimes that are not subject to amnesty or forgiveness. You know, human rights violations and crimes against humanity or terrorism.

I believe it should be an independent commission that addresses this issue, and I believe no one should beforehand state what is going to be the punishment for those who have committed crimes.

But prison would be on the table?

In a country so hurt by systematic, massive crime, the notion of impunity could be very, very dangerous because that could turn sectors of the population against the process, because people demand justice, and that’s absolutely legitimate.

What happens to lower-ranking individuals, like the guard in El Rodeo prison, who maybe engaged in torture but says they were responding to an order from above? Does that person face justice? Does that person go to prison?

You’re mentioning just one case, but this extends to practically every sector. So yes, Venezuelan society will have to make compromises so that we can move forward.

And that’s why the truth commission is so important, because we are not ignoring it. We are addressing it. Things should be known first of all, and recognition to the victims and reparations to the victims is absolutely a priority.

Do you think that the U.S. would have to enforce the results of an election? And how would it do that?

No, I don’t think so. Not today. It should have been done two years ago.

What should have happened specifically two years ago?

Well, the Venezuelan people organized, voted and proved a landslide victory on July 28, 2024. I believe the international community as a whole should have enforced that result.

Are you angry at the Biden administration for not doing more after July 2024?

I think the international community as a whole never decided to act decisively. And I think it was a horrible precedent because the message you send to societies is that at the end they are on their own.

Would you have welcomed military action by the U.S.?

Such as what happened Jan. 3, yes.

Why has the U.S. not facilitated your return to Venezuela?

There is no one other person in Venezuela that wants this three-stage process to succeed. [The United States has said its involvement in Venezuela will have three phases: stabilization, economic recovery and transition to democracy.]

I believe that my presence in Venezuela is a significant factor to help and to strengthen the success of the process.

So the fact that I go back will help channel all this growing anxiety that we’re seeing in so many demonstrations and protests.

I would say that whoever opposes my presence in Venezuela does not want the process to be successful.

Are there people in the Trump administration who also do not want you to return?

I think there are, in the United States, in different sectors, people that truly support my return, and people that have doubts that it could be done in a safe way.

The U.S. has enormous power in Venezuela. Why has Marco Rubio, for example, not facilitated your return?

I don’t know the answer in terms of his decision, but I can tell you what he has told me. And he has been very clear in terms of my right to go back to my country — and that the president had told Delcy Rodríguez that I should not be harmed when I go back. And I believe in his word.

I know you have a relationship that goes back years with Marco Rubio. What is you relationship like now? How often do you communicate?

I will keep that private because I’ve learned that in order to build long-lasting relationships you have to act with prudence.

What happened when you tried to go back to Venezuela after the June earthquakes?

Well, the first time I tried to go through Curaçao, and my plane was ordered to turn around, I was on the plane in the air. And the second time I came to Panama, I bought tickets on a commercial flight and the regime closed the air zone in Venezuela.

I just want to confirm, were there seven attempts in total to return?

Yes.

You don’t know or won’t say who was it specifically that stopped you?

I don’t know, and I prefer not to speculate, but I certainly believe that the government of Venezuela, the regime in Venezuela, was involved.

Are you concerned that coming back to Venezuela you will encounter lack of energy, fear, people becoming comfortable-ish with the situation? Are you concerned that people might not go into the streets?

Look what is happening already, and I’m not there. One the one hand, you are seeing the expressions of former political prisoners, union leaders, teachers.

They are already expressing themselves for the first time in many, many years in this way. And that’s one of the positive results of Jan. 3.

We want to turn this into a massive discussion in small assemblies, tiny assemblies, thousands of them all around the country and using technology and A.I. — we already have a platform — in order to gather all that and truly listen to what Venezuelan people are saying.

Would you keep the Chevron deal as is?

I wouldn’t be surprised if representatives of this company and others that have signed contracts right now would like to improve the terms of their contracts once we’re done.

The fact that we will have a transparent and attractive fiscal system that can be stable for the long term, and the fact we will offer international arbitration, all of this impacts directly on your rate of return and make all these investments much more profitable.

How do you get the government of Delcy Rodríguez to hand over power?

Delcy Rodríguez today follows instructions that come from the U.S. government. President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have stated a three-phase plan that includes a transition.

There are options, but certainly the fact that the U.S. has currently top members of the regime facing justice in the United States makes very clear what’s the alternative.

But a very real dilemma that you face is that by all signs Delcy Rodríguez is doing whatever the U.S. asks. The Trump administration really has enormous control to do whatever it wants in Venezuela. In a new government under María Corina Machado, the Trump administration might not be able to have so much control. Why should the Trump administration want to give up its current situation?

I do not see a dilemma there, because if you have to choose between fear and conviction in terms of your ally, your partner, you would certainly go for the second.

This Trump administration is very focused on striking deals and getting benefits as opposed to larger ideals or convictions of democracy.

I think that from every perspective you address the Venezuelan situation right now, it is a win-win situation to move ahead into the transition.

From the migration perspective, you have over a million Venezuelans in the U.S. Sixty-five percent of them say they want to go back if there is a democratic transition.

And you need to have a partner that truly is committed to dismantling the terror regime, not to try to accommodate until a later moment in which they could bring it back to the previous state.

And third, from an economic and energy perspective, yes, some deals are being made now, but it’s a fraction of what will be made once we have security, stability and legitimacy in Venezuela.

And I think the greatest legacy President Trump will have in this hemisphere is being able to have a nation that rebuilds its institutions and that turns into the strongest ally of the U.S. in the region.

When you saw President Trump come out on Jan. 3 and say, “María Corina doesn’t have the support inside the country” — after you did all of the things that we know that you did in your country — what was your response in that moment?

My assessment was that he was referring to the security forces. And I believe that certainly in the top brass, there are individuals that have persecuted me and our team for years — for years. And in that very small group certainly I do not have support.

But they [Trump officials] know better than anybody what the rest of the armed forces and the police forces in Venezuela feel and believe. Their support for our movement is huge.

Were you angry in that moment?

I was surprised.

Do you need the U.S. on your side for there to be a free and fair election?

Certainly we do. And I trust we will — we do have them. We do have the U.S. government. And I believe we have the U.S. Congress, in both parties.

But even further, I believe the American people support our cause.

This is going to work, this is going to prove to the world that even the most cruel, corrupt tyranny can be dismantled because of the will of a people and the support of democratic leaders.

And this is why this movement is so powerful, because it’s driven by values and virtues and it has to do with the truth, it has do with transparency. And it has to do with good.

And I should ask, to have it on the record, When are you going back to Venezuela?

Sooner than you would expect.

After the interview, Ms. Machado clarified some details in a phone call, and Ms. Turkewitz asked about negotiations happening between Venezuelan officials and a different faction of the opposition, which have the goal of setting an election framework.

Did you choose not to participate in these talks, or did the U.S. not invite you?

I think it is clear to everyone by now that the United States government was the one that decided how to assemble this team from both sides. And I have been very clear. I am not part of the commission; I am also not going to stand in the way. Rather — for the sake of Venezuela and for our own well-being — we all hope that what was promised is fulfilled.

item.title: Australian Lawmaker Injured After Attack, Prime Minister Says
item.description:
An Australian lawmaker was “attacked” on Monday outside her electorate office in the state of Victoria, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said, in an incident that prompted the authorities to activate the country’s counterterrorism unit.

Helen Haines, an independent lawmaker, was hit by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her office in Wangaratta, in the southern state of Victoria, on Monday at 3.35 p.m, Victoria Police said.

The driver, a 43-year-old man, “was arrested at the scene by a passerby” when he exited the car, the police said. The suspect is now in police custody and there was no threat to the broader community, according to Victoria Police’s acting superintendent, Ashley Mason. Police said a knife was found in the vehicle.

Ms. Haines, 65, was critically injured and was taken to the hospital, Victoria Police said in a statement. No further information about her condition was released.

Addressing the nation in a news conference, Mr. Albanese said the counterterrorism unit had been activated and was working with the local police, as well as the country’s spy agency. No motive had been determined, he said.

“It is too early in this investigation for me to provide you with details of what the motivation is behind this attack,” Mr. Albanese told reporters on Monday evening. “Our thoughts are with Helen and her recovery at this time.”

Speaking on television after the news conference, Mr. Albanese called on Australians to engage in respectful political debate and said the “temperature has undoubtedly increased.”

Tony Burke, the home affairs minister, said earlier that there had been 951 incidents of harassing and threatening behavior against high office holders from July 2024 to June 2025. During that same period from 2025 to 2026, there were 1,067 incidents.

Ms. Haines is an independent member of Parliament who represents the federal seat of Indi, which is in Victoria’s northeast and encompasses the cities of Wodonga, Wangaratta and Benalla.

In a statement on social media, her family said that Ms. Haines was receiving medical treatment.

“This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” said the statement. “Please keep Helen in your thoughts.”

Her family and office staff asked for privacy.

item.title: Under Siege, Ukraine Uses F-16s to Shoot Down Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones
item.description:
The skies above Ukraine now roar with the sound of F-16s targeting jet-powered drones.

Under siege and short on interceptor missiles, Ukraine is using the American-made fighter planes as a first line of defense against Russia’s deadly new weapon of choice.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine recently described the F-16 as “one of the most effective tools for shooting down” the drones, which have been menacing Ukraine’s cities. But being on constant patrol for drones that cost Russia no more than $70,000 to build is taking a toll on the multimillion-dollar fighter planes.

Ukraine’s small fleet of F-16s — about 50 in all — are in the air so often that they risk breaking down, officials and experts say. About half of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet is grounded, undergoing maintenance elsewhere in Europe, Mr. Zelensky said this month.

Kyiv is still waiting for additional F-16s that Belgium promised to donate more than three years ago. Only a few dozen Ukrainian pilots at a time can be trained to fly the jets. And running out of ammunition is a top concern.

David A. Deptula, a retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant general who is now head of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, a research group near Washington, said Ukraine was “forced to use a relatively small fighter fleet day after day as a substitute for an adequately resourced, layered air defense system.” He also noted that using the F-16s in that way meant Ukrainian forces were “consuming a finite resource faster than they should.”

“It’s not a sustainable long-term proposition,” he added.

Ukraine is rushing to develop other interceptors, but for now, the F-16s are among the few weapons Kyiv has that can keep up with the jet-powered drones and shoot them down without burning through costly Patriot missiles. The fighter jets have taken down as many as 90 percent of incoming cruise missiles in some attacks, said Col. Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force.

The reliance on F-16s has made them “critical for Ukraine,” said Lt. Gen. Krzysztof Krol, assistant to the chief of staff of Poland’s armed forces. But the fleet, he said, is “definitely insufficient.”

For Ukraine, getting F-16s was itself a battle.

The sophisticated fighter jets, made by the American defense manufacturer Lockheed Martin, require U.S. government approval to be sold or transferred abroad.

Mr. Zelensky began asking for them soon after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Some allies were willing to donate old F-16s. But the Biden administration resisted for more than a year, worried about escalating tensions between NATO and Russia and whether Ukraine could properly maintain the jets.

When Washington relented, in May 2023, it took months to begin training Ukrainian pilots to fly the jets. The first F-16s — donated by Denmark, the Netherlands and Norway — did not arrive in Ukraine until over a year later.

Since then, the planes have been airborne almost constantly, and five of them have been damaged or destroyed in battle, according to the weapons tracking site Oryx. One was shot down, killing its battle-tested pilot, Lt. Col. Oleksiy Mes, after being scrambled against a Russian air assault just weeks after the F-16s arrived in Ukraine.

The fighter planes have also racked up successes. F-16s shot down “a significant portion” of the 1,900 jet drones that Ukraine intercepted last month, out of the 3,500 that Russia launched, Colonel Ihnat said in an interview. He also said that one F-16 pilot recently shot down 10 jet-powered drones during a single flight.

The fighter jets had also intercepted 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones of different types as of late September, according to Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko, commander of the Ukrainian Air Force. And in July, an F-16 shot down a Russian Su-35 fighter jet, Colonel Ihnat said, a win for Ukraine’s overmatched force.

“Skeptics said that we would not be able to operate them from our airfields, that we would not be able to preserve them, that we would not be able to fight with them,” Colonel Ihnat said. “Where are those skeptics now?”

Though the F-16s have flown attack missions over Ukraine, firing more than 650 airstrikes against Russian ground targets, they have largely been used for air defense.

While protection from the constant pummeling of cruise missiles and drones is a priority, General Deptula, the retired U.S. general, noted, “Every F-16 sortie chasing a drone is an F-16 sortie not available for offensive counter-air missions.”

The F-16s are not equipped to launch the long-range missiles needed to put Moscow on defense — either by striking Russian military sites behind the front lines or by forcing Russian pilots to pull back.

So far, those missions have been carried out by French-made Mirages and Soviet-era warplanes that make up the rest of Ukraine’s fighter jet fleet.

Building up the fleet will take time.

Ukraine is buying 20 new Gripen fighter jets from Sweden, which is also donating 16 older models of the plane, which will arrive “soon,” Mr. Zelensky said last week. France has agreed to sell Rafale jets, though they won’t be delivered for at least two more years. Both warplanes are able to fire so-called deep strike missiles that can hit targets hundreds of kilometers into Russian territory.

Additionally, Ukraine is negotiating with Lockheed Martin to buy the newest F-16 model, which could carry longer-range missiles with U.S. government approval.

The Fetesti Air Base in southeastern Romania is the only training site outside the United States where Ukrainian pilots fly the F-16. The program at Fetesti is run by Lockheed, and training takes about six months following what is often more than a year of English language lessons and learning to fly less powerful Western jets.

Officials would not discuss how many Ukrainian pilots had completed F-16 training at air bases in the United States. But 19 pilots have graduated from the Lockheed program at Fetesti since September 2024, said Bill Thomas, a retired U.S. Air Force colonel who runs the program.

Colonel Thomas, who flew the F-16 in combat over Kosovo in 1999, said the program focused more on counter-drone missions than what NATO pilots were taught five years ago, before Russia’s war in Ukraine began.

“It’s completely different because of the nature of this changing warfare,” he said in a recent interview at the Romanian base as a Ukrainian pilot fired up his jet for a morning flight.

One of the trainees, a 25-year old Ukrainian Air Force lieutenant from the Kyiv region who spoke on condition that he be identified only by his first initial, S, was preparing to fly the F-16 solo for the first time.

He arrived in Romania in February and was still too new to have earned a call sign or nickname. Compared with slower jets he had trained on at a base in Canada, piloting the F-16 “was, like, mind-blowing,” he said.

The nature of the fighting has “completely changed almost 10 times,” during his training, he said, so Ukrainians must “be ready.”

He added: “We don’t have any choice.”

Marc Santora and Olha Konovalova contributed reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine.

item.title: For Israelis and Jews in the U.A.E., an Eroding Sense of Security
item.description:
When Tamar Smulowicz moved from Israel to the United Arab Emirates after the two countries normalized relations six years ago, it was the beginning of a chapter in a place she never dared think of as home.

Her husband had been recruited for an information technology job by the government in the port city of Ras Al Khaimah. They arrived in summer, and their daughters, then nearly 5 and 8, quickly made the pool their second home. Soon, the girls enrolled in a school with an English-language curriculum, where Ms. Smulowicz made friends with mothers from backgrounds, religions and nationalities she rarely, if ever, encountered in Israel.

“It was a once in a lifetime option,” Ms. Smulowicz said in an interview this month. “We were welcomed,” she added. “We felt safe basically from the beginning.”

But a cascade of regional wars and domestic threats is now testing the confidence of Israelis and Jews in the wealthy Gulf nation.

Today, Jewish life in the Emirates has grown quieter and less visible. Religious symbols have disappeared, and gatherings have moved into private. Many have become more guarded about their online presence and their willingness to speak to the media. Some are reconsidering how openly to identify themselves as Israeli or Jewish, while others weigh whether they can still build a life in a nation they once considered a haven.

That shift began with the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed more than 1,200 people, and Israel’s devastating war in Gaza, which killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and prompted accusations of genocide against Israel. As Israel widened its military campaigns across the region, international condemnation mounted, and Israel and Israelis faced increasing isolation.

Then, in 2024, an Israeli rabbi was kidnapped and killed in the U.A.E. Three Uzbek nationals were initially arrested in connection with the killing. Three people were later sentenced to death, while a fourth received a prison sentence. The authorities did not disclose the identities of those sentenced.

The Israeli attack on Iran in 2025, joined by the U.S., and the renewed U.S.-Israeli war in 2026, brought conflict to the doorstep. This year, Iran fired waves of missiles and drones at the Emirates, striking or sending debris into several sites, including airports and hotels. For Israeli and Jewish residents, not only was the country where they lived under attack, but Israeli officials were warning that Iran could specifically target them.

In late September, after what the authorities said was an aborted plot to crash a jetliner from Dubai to Tel Aviv in a Sept. 11-inspired suicide mission, the sense of alarm grew more intense. The low-cost carrier FlyDubai had become a major operator on the Dubai-Tel Aviv route, running as many as 10 daily flights.

Together, these events have shaken the U.A.E.’s image as a place where Jewish life could flourish openly and securely, according to several Israelis and Jewish members living in the Emirates. Community members say some people have left. Many others, like Ms. Smulowicz and her family, have stayed, learning to lead their lives with caution.

It’s “a moment of sobriety,” said Rabbi Yehuda Sarna, who previously served as the chief rabbi of the Jewish Council of the Emirates, and lectures at the New York University campus in the capital, Abu Dhabi.

For years, Israelis and Jews, traveling on Western or other foreign passports, had come to the Emirates to live and work. A small network took shape, even renting a villa to use as a synagogue.

After the U.A.E. and Israel normalized relations under the Abraham Accords in 2020, Emirati officials embraced the community’s growth, pledged to protect it and even introduced Holocaust education into school curricula.

The new warmth was not universal. Even before the Gaza war, a poll by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy in April 2023 found that 69 percent of Emiratis surveyed believed the Abraham Accords would negatively affect the region. But there was no public protest in the Emirates, an authoritarian country where the government brooks no dissent and where most residents are foreign nationals dependent on work visas.

Soon after, Israelis, both secular and religious, began arriving in the Emirates. Yarmulkes appeared on city streets. Families and friends gathered to braid challah, the traditional Jewish bread. Weddings and Passover dinners, some drawing hundreds, were held in public. Kosher restaurants and grocery stores opened, their signs visible to passers-by. In early 2023, the Abrahamic Family House, a complex that includes a mosque, a church and a synagogue, opened in Abu Dhabi.

“That was a huge renaissance,” said Marcy Grossman, director of the American Jewish Committee in Abu Dhabi, who also served as Canada’s ambassador to the U.A.E. from 2019 to 2022. “Everyone was blown away.”

The growth soon showed up in the numbers, from trade to tourism.

The U.A.E. foreign ministry reported more than $14.5 billion in trade between Israel and the U.A.E. from Sept. 2020 through May 2026.

At least 120 weekly flights also operated directly between the two countries during periods of normal service, the ministry said, with passenger traffic between the two countries reaching approximately 1.53 million in 2025.

The influx of visitors inspired Ms. Smulowicz and her partner, Ania Skinder, a Polish-Australian national, to start Adventurous Camel in July 2023, offering tours in Hebrew, Polish and English. They wanted to showcase Ras Al Khaimah’s heritage and quieter appeal as an alternative to the glitz of Dubai and Abu Dhabi.

For a time, the momentum seemed unstoppable. More Israelis arrived, more businesses opened, more families put down roots.

Then came the Oct. 7 attack on Israel and the subsequent war in Gaza, leaving Israelis anxious about their status in the U.A.E. and the future of their business.

“It was scary,” Ms. Smulowicz said. “You didn’t know what happens next.”

Since the Oct. 7 assault, Israelis have kept a lower profile, often at the encouragement of Emirati officials, several community members told The New York Times. Many people contacted for this article declined to speak or agreed to do so only on the condition of anonymity for security reasons.

Restaurants and cafes removed signs advertising their kosher offerings and scaled back or removed their social media presence. At one kosher grocery store, the blinds were drawn and a security guard photographed shoppers’ passports or identification cards at the door.

Outside a Jewish nursery school, guards in dark sunglasses stood watch as a police car sat nearby. Jewish and Israeli leaders said that some entrepreneurs seeking investment in Dubai had grown cautious about revealing their identities.

Jewish residents brought inside their mezuzas, small containers with biblical scrolls traditionally affixed to door posts. The Abrahamic Family House in Abu Dhabi, among the few places Jewish worshipers could gather and publicly pray, closed at the onset of the war on Iran.

The U.A.E. foreign ministry said in a statement that it upholds the “safety, security, and well-being of all members of society, without exception.” The ministry cited the “country’s enduring values of tolerance, coexistence, and respect for diversity.”

The retreat from public life has come amid a retrenchment of Jewish communities elsewhere, in response to rising antisemitism and deadly attacks targeting Jews.

“People changed the way they operate in the world,” Ms. Grossman said.

After Oct. 7 and the outbreak of war with Hamas, some in Israel moved abroad, even as residents of Gaza remained trapped in the besieged and devastated enclave. A young entrepreneur named Or Eliaz was among several Israelis who chose to move to the U.A.E. though other Israelis were starting to leave.

At the time, with economic and security concerns spiking, Mr. Eliaz said Israel was not “the right place” where a young person doing business could thrive, he said. (A friend of his was killed in the Oct. 7 attack, he said, and a cousin kidnapped. She has since been released.)

“I wanted a new and different opportunity for myself,” Mr. Eliaz said on a recent evening at a Dubai mall. “We want to stay somewhere peaceful.”

A 2022 trip to Dubai, while visiting the Gulf to attend the World Cup soccer tournament in Qatar, introduced a new life. Mr. Eliaz has since built a company producing promotional content and podcasts. His family, including his wife, father, brother, and his brother’s fiancée, has all moved to the Emirates.

His work has put him in contact with people from across the region, including Iranians and Pakistanis. He acknowledged that in the Emirates, where freedom of speech is curtailed, it was difficult to know what they really thought of him. For Mr. Eliaz, though, these limits were a trade-off he was willing to accept.

“I feel much more secure to live my life here than in Israel,” he said.

For now, the Jewish and Israeli population in the Emirates is nervously watching the war with Iran and other regional developments, unsure what might come next.

Rabbi Sarna said he hoped the pendulum would swing back, allowing them to live more openly again and with a greater sense of security in the U.A.E.

“There is this feeling that we are perhaps on the low end of a cycle,” Mr. Sarna said in a video interview from New York. “But it’s a cycle and we are going to be on our way up.”

item.title: France’s Far Right Seizes the Moment as Rioting Stuns the Country
item.description:
After riots erupted this weekend in cities across France, its centrist government blamed the main far-left party, accusing its politicians of inciting the violence. That party blamed the government, accusing it of stirring public anger through years of bad governance and heavy-handed policing.

What did the main far-right party do? It blamed both, and launched into campaign mode.

“We are paying for decades of being soft on crime, of weak authority, of the moral, psychological, and material disarmament of our internal security forces,” Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally party, said after emerging from a police station in central Paris on Sunday. He said had gone there to support police officers.

Then he addressed France’s “honest citizens” who were stunned on Sunday by the smashed storefronts and burned-out businesses destroyed by rioters the night before. He said they had a vital role to play in reinstating national stability. And that would be by voting in the coming election for his party.

“People need to wake up now,” Mr. Bardella said. “They need to make the right political choices, and in any case, we stand ready to restore order in the country.”

Sunday was a day of mourning, shock and finger pointing in France. The day before, huge peaceful protests for better school conditions and against rising living costs were overshadowed by black-clad and often masked agitators of unclear affiliation who attacked government buildings and shops across the country, sometimes stealing wine or electronics.

For the National Rally, which bills itself as the party of law and order as well as an advocate for expelling unauthorized immigrants, Sunday was also a day of political opportunity. It is six months before a presidential election that the party’s candidate, Marine Le Pen, is the favorite to win.

“The picture of France emerging this morning, in light of all the destruction, plays well into their hands,” said Bruno Cautrès, a political scientist at Sciences Po, a university in Paris. “We can clearly see that the National Rally is not a loser here.”

The party’s approach mirrors how far-right groups across Europe are presenting themselves as the solution to different kinds of social and governmental challenges. In July, Spain’s government briefly lost control of the borders of a Spanish territory in North Africa, allowing a surge of migrants and handing the country’s far-right party, Vox, a new issue to campaign on. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, is leading national polls, in part by channeling anxiety over the country’s identity.

In France this week, as Mr. Bardella criticized the government’s policing, Ms. Le Pen seized the moment to criticize Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the main far-left party, France Unbowed, and one of her main rivals for the presidency. She said “legitimate social demands” had been “hijacked by the far left and the rhetoric of Jean-Luc Mélenchon” and his colleagues, whom she accused of fostering chaos by “legitimizing violence” — an accusation that the party denies.

The riots arrived at a sensitive time in France, with the country already dealing with a daunting budget deficit and a deadlocked Parliament in which no party has a majority.

“The far right are sure to gain from this,” said Alexis Veller, 53, a filmmaker, who stopped his motorcycle on Sunday morning to take photos of broken storefront windows and tagged walls in central Paris. “We are a very fractured country,” he said. “The situation is very, very worrying.”

Political analysts cautioned that the six months until the election is a long time in politics, and that voters’ motivations are complex and rarely focused on a single issue.

Still, the violence perfectly aligned with the image the National Rally has long painted of a France divided into two and battling for survival, said Vincent Martigny, a political science professor at the University of Nice, Côte d’Azur.

The party has portrayed the country as split between the France of the city centers — filled with woke students and rioters, it says — and the “good France” in the quiet countryside, he said.

“They try to oppose these two Frances, for an obvious reason, because their electorate is not in the city centers, nor in the suburbs, they are clearly in this other France,” Mr. Martigny said, adding that “this fuels the feeling decay, of decline.”

Whether the unrest offers a long-term bump in the National Rally’s fortunes will depend, in part, on if the protests continue, he said.

On Sunday evening, Ms. Le Pen released a video address in which she painted this very picture of a divided France. She was filmed sitting behind a wooden desk, with the French flag behind her, hands clasped — the image of a president in waiting.

“I condemn the hijacking of this anger by thugs who are sowing chaos in the cities of France,” she said.

“In six months,” she said, “the French people will be able to choose a different path: That of restored authority and security.”

The National Rally supports a bigger, stronger police force, and campaigned in legislative elections in 2024 for mandatory minimum sentences and an end to reduced sentences, as well as building more prisons. It also pledged to lower the age when defendants can be tried as adults by two years, to 16, and to cut state subsidies to the parents of juvenile criminals.

Since the current wave of protests broke out in working-class suburban high schools, Mr. Bardella has condemned students causing damage to schools and expressed support for police officers injured in confrontations with protesters.

Across the Atlantic, President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who have both expressed support for Ms. Le Pen in the past, weighed in on the unrest in ways that amplified the National Rally’s critiques. Though the identities of the black-clad and masked rioters are largely unknown, the American leaders portrayed the unrest as caused by immigrants.

“France is burning!” Mr. Trump said on social media. “The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!”

Mr. Vance blamed the violence on “Western liberals” who “imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”

He added: “I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.”

Given how unpopular Mr. Trump’s government is in France, it was not clear whether those messages would help or hinder the National Rally.

At the police station on Sunday, Mr. Bardella was confronted by the area’s Green lawmaker, Pouria Amirshahi, who was touring his constituency wearing the tricolor sash of an elected official. It was scandalous, he said, that while he was working, Mr. Bardella was out campaigning.

“They spend their time, as you can see, rubbing their hands together over this violence as if their time has come,” Mr. Amirshahi said.

Mr. Amirshahi then turned to the camera.

“We in France should unite,” he said. “We should stand together in the face of the challenge ahead of us, and not fall into this pattern of division and this pornography of violence that seems to excite him right now.”

But Mr. Bardella wasn’t listening. He had already hopped into a car and left.

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: The Coverup: How a Trillion-Dollar Industry Launders Illegal Gold
item.description:
This is an illegal mine in Madagascar. Its gold is banned from the world’s legitimate marketplace.

Thousands of children work in these mines, in violation of international law.

Yet Madagascar’s gold flowed easily to market.

And the world’s gold authority helped cover it up.

Supported by

Times INVESTIGATION

The line between dirty and clean gold is an industry fiction. Wall Street and governments profit off gold from criminals, gangsters and those who exploit children.

By Justin Scheck

Visuals by Lynsey Addario

Reporting from illegal gold mines across Madagascar.

In an industry riddled with abuse, the world’s banks and governments rely on one entity to keep gangsters, warlords and human rights violators from selling gold into the mainstream market.

That group, the London Bullion Market Association, is the self-described “global authority for precious metals.” With the power to blacklist companies, the L.B.M.A. is the closest thing the multi-trillion-dollar industry has to an international regulator.

Governments rely on the association’s stamp as a sign that gold has been mined without human rights abuses, environmental devastation, financial sanctions or criminality. In the most literal sense, the L.B.M.A. sets the gold standard.

But a New York Times investigation found that the association has repeatedly allowed gold into the market that has been mined by criminals, cartel members and children. Refiners lie with impunity about the origins of their gold. The rules are pocked with exceptions and vagaries, and the L.B.M.A. has repeatedly decided not to enforce them.

And in the case of Madagascar, the L.B.M.A. helped change and backdate key paperwork that certified gold as free from abuse.

As prices skyrocketed in recent years and evidence emerged that gold was financing armed groups in Sudan and polluters in the Amazon, the industry perpetuated the notion that it kept such dirty gold out of the mainstream marketplace.

The New York Times

The Times investigation shows that the divide between “clean” and “dirty” gold is an industry fiction. There is just gold. And as Wall Street, central banks and investors stockpile and trade the precious metal, they’re profiting off a supply that includes gold from illegal sources.

That matters now more than ever. Two decades ago, when gold sold at about $600 an ounce, it was not profitable to drive mining barges into the deepest parts of the Amazon or use bulldozers to tear up acres of Madagascar rice fields to find gold. The price this year crossed the $5,000 mark. That has made it profitable to mine in inefficient, destructive and politically destabilizing ways.

The industry works like this: Miners and brokers sell raw gold to refiners, which melt it, remove impurities, and form it into bars. The major international marketplace accepts bars only from the 67 L.B.M.A.-certified refineries. Those refiners must document the source of every ounce of gold in every bar. They are subject to independent audits to assure that their suppliers aren’t linked to criminals, child abuse or financial sanctions.

The L.B.M.A. is financed and run by the gold industry’s biggest players, including large refiners, like Asahi, and financial houses such as HSBC, Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan and Deutsche Bank.

National governments may regulate mining, but if the L.B.M.A. does not certify the gold, it becomes all but unsellable in the world’s biggest markets.

But for all its talk about being a global authority, the L.B.M.A. is mostly a paperwork collector. The association relies on refiners to inspect the mines and to self-report the details.

One way to see how the association fails to live up to its claims is to compare its public statements with what it says in private.

On the association’s website, its chief executive, Ruth Crowell, declares, “We’re the standard-setting organization that defines how precious metals are refined, as well as traded around the world.”

In court documents in London, where Tanzanians are suing the L.B.M.A. over violence in a mine, the group disavows those very words: “The assertion that the L.B.M.A. is ‘the standard-setting organization that defines how precious metals are refined and traded around the world’ is denied.”

Ms. Crowell wrote in 2024 that the L.B.M.A. was a global authority that sets standards for “85 percent to 90 percent of the global gold production.”

In court, the association says it is “a small, not-for-profit organization” that “does not possess the levels of staff, the expertise or the resources necessary” to be held responsible for what happens in gold mines.

In an interview and written statement, Ms. Crowell said the L.B.M.A. held refiners to “the highest level of international guidelines.” But she downplayed the association’s responsibility.

“The L.B.M.A.’s role is we designate what is acceptable for entry into one market,” she said. It is up to governments to oversee the industry, she said.

With few industry guardrails, gangs have diversified from cocaine into gold. Islamist terrorist groups have gotten into the business. Russia and Iran use gold to prop up their wartime governments.

And a few years back, Madagascar’s central bank decided to capitalize on booming prices by buying and stockpiling gold, including from illegal mines that employ children.

The Madagascar case reveals how the L.B.M.A. failed in its oversight mission, the one on which the entire mainstream gold industry rests.

To see how it happened, I began at the mines themselves. I took a propeller plane from the capital, Antananarivo, and drove three hours through farmland to a mine called Madagold. The mine sits in a dry valley in the northern part of the island, surrounded by a busy market fueled by gold-rush cash.

Miners have worked here for generations, but the increase in gold price in recent years has created a bustling unlicensed operation.

The L.B.M.A. says it bans gold that “is likely to harm the health, safety or morals of children.”

Everywhere I looked, at Madagold and at mines across the country, children were in danger.

Children drank from a wastewater pipe.

Others panned for gold in pools of raw sewage.

These young women say they’ve been mining crocodile-infested waters since they were 10 and 13.

There’s no age requirement. “Anyone can do it,” the owner of one mine told us. “And I keep a share.”

Children in Madagascar’s mines crushed rocks and hauled buckets of ore. Toddlers wandered between 100-foot-deep shafts.

Rising gold prices have fueled such rogue operations around the world. Miners linked to a Colombian drug cartel have sold gold into the U.S. Mint’s supply chain, via an L.B.M.A.-certified refiner. An illegal mine in Papua New Guinea was busy with child workers this month. A manager showed me a receipt. He was selling to a subsidiary of a major L.B.M.A.-certified refiner.

The association says that mines must be licensed and legal, and that they cannot destroy the environment. But illegal mines and environmental damage were rampant across Madagascar.

In the gold-rich northern region of Diana, miners follow no laws, the government’s regional mining supervisor, Firmin Razafindratondra, said. All of the area’s gold mining, he said, is illegal.

Outside Mananjary, on Madagascar’s east coast, miners operated despite government shutdown orders. Excavators turned rice paddies into a giant pit. In the north, workers felled trees in a protected forest to make beams for mine shafts. Such destruction plays out around the country.

“The environment is destroyed,” Elys Karena Hanitriniaina, the governor of another gold-mining region, said.

So there were obvious signs, to anyone who visited, that Madagascar’s mines would be hard-pressed to meet L.B.M.A. standards. Yet the gold breezed onto the market.

Here’s how it happened.

Several years ago, Madagascar’s central bank decided to start a national gold stockpile. Bank representatives bought gold from around the country. Government documents show that some came from Madagold, the mine where children worked and drank from wastewater pipes.

Other gold came, Madagold’s chief executive said, came from muddy pits nearby. When I visited, toddlers panned for gold there. Much of the rest came from intermediaries who bought from informal mines.

For that gold to be worth anything, it needed to be “certified L.B.M.A.,” Madagascar’s central bank governor, Aivo Andrianarivelo, said.

So he dispatched his gold chief to Switzerland to find a refiner. Initially, it did not go well. Refiners questioned the gold’s origins and legality, Mr. Andrianarivelo said. “The answer we gave them didn’t give enough satisfaction or trust to the Swiss,” he said.

“Nobody wanted to touch this gold,” said Marc Ummel, a gold-supply-chain specialist at the nonprofit group SwissAid who met with Madagascar’s representative during the trip.

This was an example of the system working.

Small-scale mines are considered red flags. The L.B.M.A.’s rules say that any refiner accepting this gold would be required to conduct mine inspections. Swiss refiners worried that the bank couldn’t even identify all its sources.

Even if it could have, the required inspections would have revealed children, pollution and criminality. “‘It’s impossible,’” Mr. Ummel remembers telling Madagascar’s banker. “You will never be able to find an L.B.M.A. refiner.’”

On that point, he was wrong.

The central bank cut a deal in 2023 with the Istanbul Gold Refinery, one of the world’s biggest L.B.M.A.-certified refiners.

The Turkish refiner’s auditor filed paperwork with the L.B.M.A. claiming that it “does not do any business” with mines that raise red flags, records reviewed by The Times show. That claim freed the company from having to conduct inspections.

In an interview, Mr. Andrianarivelo acknowledged that children worked in Madagascar’s mines and said that his understanding was that they provided support work to miners, rather than hammering rock themselves. He acknowledged, too, that the mines did not follow safety laws. The workers, he said, were “very small and very poor people” who believed that only God, not safety equipment, would protect them.

The raw gold was melted into 12 kg bars at a plant next to Madagascar’s international airport. From there, tens of millions of dollars in gold was shipped to Turkey to enter the legitimate supply.

Normally, once the Turkish refiner filed the paperwork with the L.B.M.A., that would be the end of it. Unless discrepancies surface — from whistle-blowers, journalists or law enforcement authorities, for example — the L.B.M.A. does not typically independently verify that the paperwork matches the reality.

When discrepancies do surface, the refiners seldom face serious consequences.

Three years ago, for example, the L.B.M.A. learned that a refiner had received illegally mined gold from the Amazon. The refiner blamed the supplier, and the association took no action.

When an Australian refiner bought gold tied to child labor and other abuses in Papua New Guinea, the association blacklisted the auditor, not the refiner. The L.B.M.A. said it required the refiner to make unspecified management improvements. But the gold still sold.

And in 2021, emails show, the L.B.M.A. learned that Istanbul Gold Refinery itself had received gold originating from small-scale mines in Mauritania, where forced labor is well documented. The refiner did not disclose this and reported no inspections. The association determined that the refiner had broken no rules.

It was only by chance that anyone at the L.B.M.A. took a look at the Madagascar gold. The European Union happened to be considering certifying the association for a new oversight role. An E.U. inspector noticed the Madagascar deal and began scrutinizing it.

How, the inspector asked, could a refinery process gold from Madagascar yet claim no red flags? UNICEF has reported more than 230,000 children working in the country’s mines. The Justice Department and the International Monetary Fund have documented industry abuses there.

L.B.M.A. staff escalated the problem to a “compliance panel” that included the chief executive, Ms. Crowell. The association could have punished the refiner. Instead, the L.B.M.A. helped cover up the problem.

Association officials worked with the Istanbul Gold Refinery’s auditor to create a new report that made it seem like the refiner had disclosed the red flags from the beginning and had taken steps to scrutinize the supply chain, according to documents and the refiner.

The second report acknowledged that the company bought gold that originated in small-scale, red flag operations. But the report concluded that the mines “do not use child labor.”

The report was backdated, as if it had been filed in real time.

That backdated report remains on the L.B.M.A.’s website, with no indication of any alterations. The document serves as proof that Istanbul Gold Refinery processed only gold that had no connection to child labor or other abuses — claims that are undercut by what I saw in the mines.

A close look at the backdated report shows that, even with the changes, the Istanbul Gold Refinery did not follow L.B.M.A. rules as written. Those rules require refiners who process high-risk gold either to inspect the mines themselves or to use independent third parties to do so. The Istanbul refiner relied instead on the seller, the central bank, to self-certify that no child labor was used.

The rules as written make no allowance for such a self-certification. But Mustafa Salali, the Istanbul Gold Refinery’s compliance officer, told me that, in this case, he relied on the word of a government entity, the bank. As far as he was concerned, he said, everything was by the book because the L.B.M.A. signed off on the audit.

In response to questions about the backdated audit, Ms. Crowell acknowledged “non-conformances” in the process and said that “the chronology of these documents could have been explained more clearly.”

Initially, she said the refinery had been punished by being subjected to a publicly announced compliance investigation. She later said that no such investigation had actually been announced.

She said that the L.B.M.A. had mandated a “corrective action plan” — but the refiner said all it had to do was update the report.

The matter was closed. The gold was certified as meeting the world’s most rigorous standards.

It all worked out quite well for Madagascar’s destructive and exploitative gold industry.

Back when Mr. Andrianarivelo was shopping gold in Switzerland, many companies had turned him away. Now those same refiners are calling him looking to buy gold, he said, because the L.B.M.A. had declared that “there was no issue” with it.
